analysis.title: Ruminations - Macro, Micro, Markets (Bobby Molavi, 9 Nov 2026)
key_insights: The S&P 500 fell 2.68% on the week to 7,377, the Nasdaq 3.37%, the Dow 0.94% and the Russell 2.05%. The author describes three different markets in three sessions: a post-election relief rally on Wednesday, an air-pocket gap lower on Thursday, and some bottom-dipping on Friday.

The author's primary driver for the week was a negative feedback loop between performance and technicals. Pnl losses triggered technical stops, short-duration leveraged strategies were forced to degross, and the selling hit the same references that had triggered the degrossing, which produced further selling.

Wednesday's rally treated the Democratic sweep of both chambers as benign because gridlock is historically stock-friendly. Thursday's selloff was pinned partly on fears of tighter AI and data-center regulation under the new Congress, so the election added to AI anxiety.

Thursday was an air pocket: the S&P fell 4.4%, the Dow 1,833 points and the Nasdaq 6.3%, its worst session since the pandemic reaction. The VIX spiked about 70%, all eleven sectors closed red, and Nvidia lost more than $440bn of market value.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell over 12% on the week. The largest decliners were Lumentum -36%, Seagate -28%, Marvell -28%, Western Digital -28% and SanDisk -27%. The AI buildout complex that led on the way up is leading on the way down.

The author lists four anchors: the AI debate (now including the effect of the Democratic sweep), oil moving lower (GDP slowdown, no Middle East escalation, a calmer political backdrop), yields normalising as the market prices a possible AI capex slowdown, lower oil and the effect of the last hike, and earnings that remain solid but are not enough to support prices.
H1 and Q2 2026 were a market where everyone got paid, similar to 2021. Q3 and Q4 so far have been much harder, and participants have lost much of what they made in H1.

Gross and basis became close to impossible to manage last week. Spreads widened and correlations broke down in software vs semis, Apple vs Nasdaq, banks vs insurance, European banks vs European defence, defensives vs growth, small vs large cap, Europe vs US, and S&P ex-AI vs S&P.

Rotation has continued for several weeks into value, small and mid cap, under-owned, defensive and real-economy stocks. Staples, real estate, healthcare, consumer and travel offset AI and tech drawdowns in the S&P. The S&P had been up 12-13% on the year while most of its stocks were down.

Technicals, positioning and performance were the main story. Gross exposure had come down but concentration had not. Pnl drawdowns drove gross lower, and AI-vs-index hedges did not work as hedges. Long/short funds have had a very hard 4 to 6 weeks, and the losses have spread to multi-asset, systematic, credit and convertible strategies.

Goldman's prime brokerage risk team found that realized 3-month alpha correlations between Fundamental and Systematic L/S managers were in the top decile of the past decade coming out of summer. Correlations between US and Asia Fundamental managers reached all-time highs, largely because of the AI trade.

Index concentration and the growth of passive, ETF, market-neutral and systematic money have made momentum a factor present in every portfolio. Over 60% of YTD returns six months into the year came from 6 stocks, and 35% from 1 stock. Nvidia went from $1 trillion to $5.8 trillion at its peak and then to close to $4 trillion within weeks.

The author separates bubbles from the usefulness of the underlying technology. In earlier capital-heavy cycles (railways, telecom and internet infrastructure) the technology reshaped the economy, but early capital was hurt and value did not always go to the builders. He frames the open question for AI as the price of innovation and the timing of returns, not its value.

AI has an unusual degree of circularity and interdependence, with examples such as the Nvidia and OpenAI deal, Nvidia's stake in Intel, Oracle's use of Nvidia GPUs, and hyperscalers' stakes in AI startups.

On valuation, the S&P settled at about 18x forward P/E last week. The author gives earlier trough forward P/Es of 10.4x (March 2009), 13.3x (March 2020) and 15.7x (October 2022), and concludes the market is cheaper rather than cheap. These multiples do not include growth rates.
The author flags a market move in Nvidia on Monday after weekend news. The note does not say what the news was.

Chart notes: the Vol Panic Index had its biggest 2-day round trip on record, and semis are down about 28% over one month, one of the largest rolling 1-month drawdowns in history. Per Pete Callahan, a key support level was touched and held so far, and the valuation premium of S&P staples to the SPX is the highest in 10+ years.
QQQ set a notional volume record of $86 billion. The author says volume and liquidity are different things.
Last Wednesday and Thursday were a $3tr event: total US market cap fell from $75tr to under $72tr. US market cap is still up about $5tr (about 7%) YTD. Momentum, the leading factor, had a wobble.

market_movers.rationale: Nvidia lost more than $440bn of market value on Thursday. The note flags a further move on Monday on weekend news and describes a fall from $5.8 trillion at the peak to close to $4 trillion.
Lumentum fell 36% on the week, the largest decline among the AI buildout names the author lists.
Seagate fell 28% on the week as part of the AI buildout unwind.
Marvell fell 28% on the week as part of the AI buildout unwind.
Western Digital fell 28% on the week as part of the AI buildout unwind.
SanDisk fell 27% on the week as part of the AI buildout unwind.

sector_views.rationale: The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell over 12% on the week and about 28% over one month, one of the largest rolling 1-month drawdowns in history. The author does not issue a formal rating.

Staples outperformed during the rotation. Per Pete Callahan, their valuation premium to the SPX is the highest in 10+ years, and the sector trades at about 2x the 24-month forward multiple of semiconductors.

sector_views.sector: Defensives, value, small and mid cap
sector_views.rationale: The author describes several weeks of rotation into value, small and mid cap, under-owned, defensive and real-economy stocks. The note describes flows and does not recommend a position.

earnings_insights: Earnings are described as still very solid, and in some cases blowout, but that is not enough to support share prices. The note gives no company-level EPS or revenue figures.

macro_indicators.interpretation: The author attributes the move to a GDP slowdown, no escalation in the Middle East, talk of talks, and a Democratic win pointing to calmer conditions.
The author attributes this to the market pricing a possible AI capex slowdown, lower oil and the effective tightening from the last hike.
The author calls the market cheaper rather than cheap compared with earlier troughs of 10.4x, 13.3x and 15.7x, and notes that growth rates are not in the comparison.

risk_factors: Further forced selling and degrossing if tight stops and high leverage are hit again in a crowded, concentrated market.
Tighter AI and data-center regulation under the new Congress.
Concentration: a handful of stocks drove most of the year's index returns, so a reversal in those names hits index-tracking money.
Circular financing and interdependence among AI companies.
Whether Friday's stabilisation was momentary or a new floor. The author calls this week key.

tension_points.bull_case: Earnings remain very solid and in some cases blowout. The S&P at 18x forward P/E is cheaper than recent history. Friday's bottom-dipping and a support level that held could mark a floor. Innovation has lasting value even after bubbles.
tension_points.bear_case: Solid earnings are not enough to hold prices. Forced degrossing, crowding and momentum unwinds can continue. Semis are down about 28% in a month, and AI financing is circular. Early capital in past bubbles was hurt.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Whether Friday's pause was momentary or a new floor. The author calls this week key.

theme_stances.evidence: negative reinforcing feedback loop between performance and technicals

theme_stances.key_argument: Passive and systematic money and the growth of momentum as a factor push concentrated winners up and can reverse the same way on the way down.
theme_stances.evidence: that is what can take you from $5.8 trillion to close to $4 trillion

theme_stances.key_argument: Several weeks of rotation into value, small and mid cap and defensive names have offset AI and tech drawdowns in the S&P.
